    WHAT THIS ACTUALLY PROVES

    Consistency is a starting point.

    A candidate can satisfy every rule while other candidates do too. Exhaustive enumeration establishes uniqueness only over the nine declared integers. An inconsistent rulebook has no valid answer; this lab does not draw conclusions from it.

    This is a symbolic sandbox, not a trained neural network or a formal proof assistant. The PINN experiment trains real networks. Here, exact enumeration isolates what constraints can and cannot establish.

    BEYOND PHYSICS

    The rules need evidence too.

    In physics, conservation laws can constrain a prediction, while missing boundary conditions leave it ambiguous. In physiology, balance equations need patient-specific parameters and measurements. In psychology, behavioral regularities are often probabilistic and context-dependent.

    Mathematical conclusions follow from specified axioms and sound reasoning. Claims about the world also depend on whether the assumptions describe it. “Wrong rule” makes that distinction visible: a uniquely valid answer can disagree with the held-out observation.

    Soft penalties are inspired by Ben Moseley’s PINN introduction. Rule weights and penalty formulas are modeling choices, not levels of truth.
